scenes.tts: Every time this egg divides, it destroys one of its own proteins. Then it builds it up again. Why would a cell destroy its engine's partner, every single time?
scenes.narration: Every time this egg divides, it destroys one of its own proteins. Then it builds it up again. Why would a cell destroy its engine's partner, every single time?
scenes.caption: Every time this egg divides, it destroys one of its own proteins. Then it builds it up again. Why would a cell destroy its engine's partner, every single time?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, built here and kept for the whole film. Left 60%: one large round cell in cross-section (grey outline, gently breathing), filling about 70% of frame height, with a grey nucleus. Label above it: 'sea-urchin egg'. Right 40%: the record, a chart with a time axis and a white scrubber line that moves left to right at a steady pace; small label 'schematic' in its corner. As the scrubber moves, small orange rounded shapes labelled 'cyclin' multiply inside the cell and an ORANGE trace climbs on the chart in step. When the scrubber reaches division, the cell pinches in two; the orange shapes flash RED and vanish; the orange trace drops straight to the floor. The right daughter slides off-frame and the left daughter swells back to full size in the same place. Repeat once more so a sawtooth of two teeth is drawn. On 'Why would a cell', the question appears across the top in white: 'Why destroy it every time?'

Title 'One Rise, One Fall' fades in over the top of the world for 2 s while the scrubber keeps moving and orange cyclin shapes begin building again inside the cell. The question text from the hook fades out under it.

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty-two, at Woods Hole, Tim Hunt's group saw this in dividing sea-urchin eggs. The protein climbed through each cycle and vanished at every division. They named it cyclin. The eggs make it all the time. It falls because it is destroyed.
scenes.narration: In 1982, at Woods Hole, Tim Hunt's group saw this in dividing sea-urchin eggs. The protein climbed through each cycle and vanished at every division. They named it cyclin. The eggs make it all the time. It falls because it is destroyed.
scenes.caption: In 1982, at Woods Hole, Tim Hunt's group saw this in dividing sea-urchin eggs. The protein climbed through each cycle and vanished at every division. They named it cyclin. The eggs make it all the time. It falls because it is destroyed.
scenes.visual: The scrubber draws a third orange tooth on the record. On 'They named it cyclin', the orange label 'cyclin' on the chart trace pulses. On 'make it all the time', new orange shapes keep appearing at a steady trickle inside the cell (a small ribosome-like dot emits them; no structure). On 'destroyed', the division comes again: the orange shapes flash RED and break into fragments that fade, and the trace drops. Daughter swap as before. Small caption under the chart: 'Hunt and colleagues, 1982 to 1983'.

scenes.tts: Cyclin's partner is a kinase, a C D K, or cyclin-dependent kinase. Alone, the C D K is inactive. A bound cyclin is needed to switch it on. Every eukaryotic cell, from yeast to human, runs its cycle on this engine.
scenes.narration: Cyclin's partner is a kinase, a CDK, or cyclin-dependent kinase. Alone, the CDK is inactive. A bound cyclin is needed to switch it on. Every eukaryotic cell, from yeast to human, runs its cycle on this engine.
scenes.caption: Cyclin's partner is a kinase, a CDK, or cyclin-dependent kinase. Alone, the CDK is inactive. A bound cyclin is needed to switch it on. Every eukaryotic cell, from yeast to human, runs its cycle on this engine.
scenes.visual: Inside the same cell, three BLUE rounded shapes labelled 'CDK' drift into view near the nucleus, each with a dark, closed notch; they stay at a constant number (CDK level steady). Show first, then name. On 'needed to switch it on', an orange cyclin shape docks onto one CDK and that pair gains a soft GREEN rim (on). The other CDKs, without cyclin, stay dark. On 'from yeast to human', the cell label above changes from 'sea-urchin egg' to 'any eukaryotic cell' (morph the text, do not cut). The scrubber keeps moving; the orange trace keeps rising.

scenes.tts: Now add a second trace: the kinase's activity. In cycles like a frog embryo's first, it does not follow the ramp. It stays low through most of interphase. Then it can snap up just before mitosis, and crash as cyclin is destroyed.
scenes.narration: Now add a second trace: the kinase's activity. In cycles like a frog embryo's first, it does not follow the ramp. It stays low through most of interphase. Then it can snap up just before mitosis, and crash as cyclin is destroyed.
scenes.caption: Now add a second trace: the kinase's activity. In cycles like a frog embryo's first, it does not follow the ramp. It stays low through most of interphase. Then it can snap up just before mitosis, and crash as cyclin is destroyed.
scenes.visual: The scrubber returns to the left of the record and replays one cycle. A GREEN trace labelled 'CDK activity' is drawn beside the orange one: flat and low while orange ramps, then a near-vertical rise just before the division mark, then a drop with the orange. Label 'schematic' stays visible. In the cell, the orange-blue pairs pile up with no green rim while the green trace is flat; at the snap they all light GREEN at once; at the crash the orange shapes flash RED and vanish and the green rims go out. A phase tag above the cell reads G1, S, G2, M in step with the scrubber.

scenes.tts: Here is the puzzle. Cyclin climbs steadily, and cyclin switches the kinase on. So why does the activity wait, and then jump?
scenes.narration: Here is the puzzle. Cyclin climbs steadily, and cyclin switches the kinase on. So why does the activity wait, and then jump?
scenes.caption: Here is the puzzle. Cyclin climbs steadily, and cyclin switches the kinase on. So why does the activity wait, and then jump?
scenes.visual: The scrubber stops just before the snap. The stretch where orange climbs but green stays flat is shaded in a soft band on the record. Inside the cell, the many orange-blue pairs sit dark and pulse gently. Question card at top in white: 'Why wait, then jump?'
Predict pause. The question card 'Why wait, then jump?' stays on screen. Near-stillness by design: only the dark pairs inside the cell bob slowly and the shaded band on the record shimmers.

scenes.tts: Because a pair can be built and still be held off. The mitotic pair is C D K one with cyclin B. All through G two, Wee one adds an inhibitory phosphate to each new pair. Inactive pairs pile up, loaded and waiting.
scenes.narration: Because a pair can be built and still be held off. The mitotic pair is CDK1 with cyclin B. All through G2, Wee1 adds an inhibitory phosphate to each new pair. Inactive pairs pile up, loaded and waiting.
scenes.caption: Because a pair can be built and still be held off. The mitotic pair is CDK1 with cyclin B. All through G2, Wee1 adds an inhibitory phosphate to each new pair. Inactive pairs pile up, loaded and waiting.
scenes.visual: Question card dissolves. The phase tag reads G2. A PURPLE shape labelled 'Wee1' moves among the pairs; each time a new orange-blue pair forms, Wee1 touches it and a GOLD badge (the inhibitory phosphate) pops onto it. Pairs collect into a growing heap, each carrying a gold badge, all dark. The pair label reads 'CDK1 + cyclin B'. On the record the scrubber creeps forward: orange keeps rising, green stays flat.

scenes.tts: Then a phosphatase, C D C twenty-five, takes the phosphate off. Once a little C D K one escapes, it boosts C D C twenty-five and slows Wee one. Each active pair frees more. Activity does not creep; it snaps, all or none.
scenes.narration: Then a phosphatase, Cdc25, takes the phosphate off. Once a little CDK1 escapes, it boosts Cdc25 and slows Wee1. Each active pair frees more. Activity does not creep; it snaps, all or none.
scenes.caption: Then a phosphatase, Cdc25, takes the phosphate off. Once a little CDK1 escapes, it boosts Cdc25 and slows Wee1. Each active pair frees more. Activity does not creep; it snaps, all or none.
scenes.visual: A second PURPLE shape labelled 'Cdc25' enters and plucks a gold badge off one pair, which lights GREEN. That green pair sends a short green arrow to Cdc25 (Cdc25 grows brighter) and a green blunt bar to Wee1 (Wee1 dims and shrinks). Cdc25 now plucks faster; badges fly off the heap in an accelerating cascade and the whole heap turns GREEN within about a second. On the record the scrubber resumes and the green trace snaps up at the same moment. Phase tag turns to M; inside the cell the nucleus outline dissolves and chromosomes condense as simple grey X shapes.

scenes.tts: Checkpoints pull the same levers. If DNA is damaged or unfinished in G two, sensor kinases switch off C D C twenty-five. C D K one keeps its brake, and the cell waits.
scenes.narration: Checkpoints pull the same levers. If DNA is damaged or unfinished in G2, sensor kinases switch off Cdc25. CDK1 keeps its brake, and the cell waits.
scenes.caption: Checkpoints pull the same levers. If DNA is damaged or unfinished in G2, sensor kinases switch off Cdc25. CDK1 keeps its brake, and the cell waits.
scenes.visual: Rewind the world gently to G2 (the scrubber slides back, chromosomes relax, nucleus reforms, gold badges return to the dark heap). A TEAL DNA strand inside the nucleus shows a small RED break. A shape labelled 'sensor kinases' appears at the break and sends a red blunt bar to Cdc25, which greys out. The gold badges stay on; the heap stays dark. On the record the scrubber holds at G2, the orange trace keeps creeping up and the green trace stays flat: a labelled 'wait' stretch. Then the break mends (red mark fades) and the scrubber moves on.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. C D K activity rises and falls once per cycle. The rise carries the cell from G one, through S, into mitosis. Destroying cyclin brings the fall. And that one rise and fall copies the genome once.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. CDK activity rises and falls once per cycle. The rise carries the cell from G1, through S, into mitosis. Destroying cyclin brings the fall. And that one rise and fall copies the genome once.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. CDK activity rises and falls once per cycle. The rise carries the cell from G1, through S, into mitosis. Destroying cyclin brings the fall. And that one rise and fall copies the genome once.
scenes.visual: The record now shows exactly one full cycle of the green trace, with the scrubber running across it once. A thick GREEN up-arrow labelled 'rise' rides the climb, synced with the phase tag ticking G1, S, G2, M; a thick RED down-arrow labelled 'fall' rides the drop. Inside the cell, the matching events play in miniature: the heap lights, chromosomes condense, then orange shapes flash RED and vanish. On 'copies the genome once', the nucleus's teal DNA shows a single copy forming (one strand becomes two, once). Large white text appears over the record and stays through the scene: 'Rises and falls once per cycle'.

scenes.tts: Now the fall. It starts with one enzyme: the A P C, or anaphase-promoting complex. Until every chromosome grips the spindle, a checkpoint holds the APC back. The cell waits before anaphase.
scenes.narration: Now the fall. It starts with one enzyme: the APC/C, or anaphase-promoting complex. Until every chromosome grips the spindle, a checkpoint holds the APC/C back. The cell waits before anaphase.
scenes.caption: Now the fall. It starts with one enzyme: the APC/C, or anaphase-promoting complex. Until every chromosome grips the spindle, a checkpoint holds the APC/C back. The cell waits before anaphase.
scenes.visual: The scrubber sits at the top of the green peak; phase tag reads M. Inside the cell the grey X chromosomes gather toward the middle; thin grey spindle lines reach in from two poles. Pairs of sister chromatids are held by small GREY rings labelled 'cohesin', with a PINK shape labelled 'securin' guarding them. A large RED shape labelled 'APC' sits beside them, held by a thin tether. One chromosome is not yet attached and blinks; the tether stays taut. Then its spindle line reaches it, the blinking stops, and the tether loosens.

scenes.tts: Once the checkpoint falls silent, the APC tags two proteins for destruction. Securin goes, so the sister chromatids separate. Cyclin B goes, so activity falls and the cell leaves mitosis.
scenes.narration: Once the checkpoint falls silent, the APC/C tags two proteins for destruction. Securin goes, so the sister chromatids separate. Cyclin B goes, so activity falls and the cell leaves mitosis.
scenes.caption: Once the checkpoint falls silent, the APC/C tags two proteins for destruction. Securin goes, so the sister chromatids separate. Cyclin B goes, so activity falls and the cell leaves mitosis.
scenes.visual: The tether drops. The RED APC shape reaches two targets and sticks a small red tag on each: the PINK securin and the ORANGE cyclin. On 'Securin goes', securin breaks into fragments that fade; the grey cohesin rings open and the sister chromatids slide apart toward the two poles. On 'Cyclin B goes', the orange shapes break up and fade; the blue CDKs left behind go dark. On the record the scrubber moves on and both traces fall to the floor together. The cell pinches in two; the daughter swap carries one cell forward, nucleus reforming.

scenes.tts: Why not just switch the kinase off? A phosphate can be removed; that is only a pause. A destroyed protein cannot be switched back on. It must be made again. That is a main reason the big transitions run one way.
scenes.narration: Why not just switch the kinase off? A phosphate can be removed; that is only a pause. A destroyed protein cannot be switched back on. It must be made again. That is a main reason the big transitions run one way.
scenes.caption: Why not just switch the kinase off? A phosphate can be removed; that is only a pause. A destroyed protein cannot be switched back on. It must be made again. That is a main reason the big transitions run one way.
scenes.visual: Split the cell's interior into two side-by-side lanes for this scene only (the cell outline stays). Left lane: a gold badge pops onto a pair and off again, back and forth, labelled 'pause'. Right lane: an orange cyclin breaks into red fragments that fade; nothing comes back until a new orange shape is slowly built from the steady trickle, labelled 'made again'. On the record, a one-way arrow sweeps forward along the time axis. On 'one way', the two lanes merge back into the single cell.

scenes.tts: Here is the test. Frog egg extracts cycle in a tube. Give them a cyclin that cannot be destroyed. What happens?
scenes.narration: Here is the test. Frog egg extracts cycle in a tube. Give them a cyclin that cannot be destroyed. What happens?
scenes.caption: Here is the test. Frog egg extracts cycle in a tube. Give them a cyclin that cannot be destroyed. What happens?
scenes.visual: The cell's outline morphs into a test tube in the same place, its contents still showing the blue CDKs and orange cyclins (label 'frog egg extract'). The record keeps running: one normal sawtooth cycle plays. Then a new ORANGE shape with a thick outline and a small lock icon, labelled 'cannot be destroyed', is dropped in. Question card at top: 'What happens?'
Predict pause. 'What happens?' stays on screen. The locked cyclins drift slowly in the tube; the scrubber creeps forward but the next part of the traces is hidden behind a soft blur.

scenes.tts: The extract went into mitosis. The kinase stayed active, and the extract did not come out. Making cyclin drives entry. Destroying it permits exit.
scenes.narration: The extract went into mitosis. The kinase stayed active, and the extract did not come out. Making cyclin drives entry. Destroying it permits exit.
scenes.caption: The extract went into mitosis. The kinase stayed active, and the extract did not come out. Making cyclin drives entry. Destroying it permits exit.
scenes.visual: Blur lifts. The green trace rises and snaps up into mitosis as usual, then stays high and flat to the end of the axis; the orange trace stays high too. In the tube, the RED APC shape bumps the locked cyclins and they do not break; the blue CDKs stay GREEN. On 'Making cyclin drives entry', a green up-arrow labels the rise; on 'Destroying it permits exit', a red dashed down-arrow appears where the fall should have been. Then the tube morphs back into the cell outline.

scenes.tts: The same rise and fall controls copying. An origin of replication must be licensed before it can fire. Licensing happens only while activity is low, in late mitosis and G one. Firing needs the rising activity of S phase.
scenes.narration: The same rise and fall controls copying. An origin of replication must be licensed before it can fire. Licensing happens only while activity is low, in late mitosis and G one. Firing needs the rising activity of S phase.
scenes.caption: The same rise and fall controls copying. An origin of replication must be licensed before it can fire. Licensing happens only while activity is low, in late mitosis and G one. Firing needs the rising activity of S phase.
scenes.visual: Back in the cell, the record restarts at the floor of a new cycle. Two dashed horizontal lines appear on the record: a low band labelled 'license' and a higher line labelled 'fire' (both schematic). Inside the nucleus, the TEAL DNA strand shows four small teal dots, the origins. While the green trace is in the low band (phase tag G1), each dot gains a teal ring, labelled 'licensed'. When the green trace crosses the 'fire' line (phase tag S), each ringed origin opens into a small bubble that grows along the strand as copying spreads; the ring is used up.

scenes.tts: High activity also blocks new licences, in yeast, and helps block them in animal cells. So each origin can fire at most once per cycle. New licences wait for the fall, normally at mitosis.
scenes.narration: High activity also blocks new licences, in yeast, and helps block them in animal cells. So each origin can fire at most once per cycle. New licences wait for the fall, normally at mitosis.
scenes.caption: High activity also blocks new licences, in yeast, and helps block them in animal cells. So each origin can fire at most once per cycle. New licences wait for the fall, normally at mitosis.
scenes.visual: The green trace stays above the 'license' band through S and G2. A fired origin tries to take a new ring; a red blunt bar from the green trace blocks it (label 'no new licence'). Copying finishes: the strand is now two. Then the scrubber runs through mitosis, the trace falls into the low band, and the daughter cell's origins gain fresh rings again. A small counter beside the nucleus reads 'copies this cycle: 1'.

scenes.tts: Fission-yeast cells test the rule. Without their mitotic cyclin, activity falls after S phase, with no mitosis. Origins are licensed afresh, and the cells copy their DNA again, without dividing.
scenes.narration: Fission-yeast cells test the rule. Without their mitotic cyclin, activity falls after S phase, with no mitosis. Origins are licensed afresh, and the cells copy their DNA again, without dividing.
scenes.caption: Fission-yeast cells test the rule. Without their mitotic cyclin, activity falls after S phase, with no mitosis. Origins are licensed afresh, and the cells copy their DNA again, without dividing.
scenes.visual: The cell outline stretches into a rod shape in place (label 'fission yeast, no mitotic cyclin'). The record replays: green rises, origins fire, the strand becomes two; then, with no mitosis, green falls straight back into the 'license' band. Fresh rings snap onto the origins, green rises past 'fire' again, and copying runs again; the nucleus swells. The counter ticks 'copies: 2', then '3'. The rod never divides.

scenes.tts: So why destroy cyclin every time? Because the kinase must climb once and fall once per cycle. Destruction is what normally makes the fall one way. The cell leaves mitosis, resets its origins, and copies its genome once per cycle.
scenes.narration: So why destroy cyclin every time? Because the kinase must climb once and fall once per cycle. Destruction is what normally makes the fall one way. The cell leaves mitosis, resets its origins, and copies its genome once per cycle.
scenes.caption: So why destroy cyclin every time? Because the kinase must climb once and fall once per cycle. Destruction is what normally makes the fall one way. The cell leaves mitosis, resets its origins, and copies its genome once per cycle.
scenes.visual: The rod morphs back into the round cell, normal again. The record replays one clean cycle at full width: orange sawtooth, green flat-then-snap-then-crash, 'license' band and 'fire' line. As the narration names each event, its picture recurs briefly in the cell: the heap lighting GREEN, APC tagging cyclin (RED fragments fade), origins taking fresh rings. The counter reads 'copies this cycle: 1'. The hook's question text returns faintly at the top, then fades as the answer finishes.
End card
scenes.line: Make cyclin to enter mitosis; destroy it to reset, once per cycle.
